note: Subjects/9701 Chemistry/04 States of matter/4.1 The gaseous state: ideal and real gases and pV = nRT.md
outline: Moving gas molecules collide with container walls. Their momentum changes produce a force on each wall; force per unit area is pressure. Ideal particles have zero own volume and no intermolecular attraction, although they retain mass. Real gases approach this model at high temperature and low pressure. For an ideal gas, $pV=nRT$ with pressure in pascals, volume in cubic metres, temperature in kelvin and $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. For a gas of mass $m$, $n=m/M_r$, hence $M_r=mRT/(pV)$.

misconceptions.statement: Gas pressure is caused by molecules colliding with one another only.
misconceptions.refutation: Pressure on a container is force per unit area caused by collisions with its walls.
misconceptions.contrast: Each wall collision changes molecular momentum and exerts a force on the wall.

misconceptions.statement: Ideal gas molecules have no mass.
misconceptions.refutation: Their own volume is treated as zero; their mass is not zero.
misconceptions.contrast: Ideal molecules still have momentum and cause pressure.

misconceptions.statement: Intermolecular attraction does not affect departure from ideal behaviour.
misconceptions.refutation: Attractive forces make real gases deviate from the ideal model, especially at lower temperature.
misconceptions.contrast: Steam deviates more than ammonia under the stated conditions because its hydrogen bonding is stronger.

misconceptions.statement: Volume in dm³ can be inserted directly with pressure in Pa and R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
misconceptions.refutation: Convert volume to m³ so pV has units of joules.

misconceptions.statement: Moles of gas from pV=nRT always equal moles of the starting reagent.
misconceptions.refutation: Use the balanced equation after calculating gas moles.
misconceptions.contrast: Four KNO₃ units form eight gas molecules, so KNO₃ amount is half the gas amount.

flashcards.front: State the ideal gas equation and the value of $R$.

9701-4.1.1.motivate: Why does an inflated tyre push on its walls even when the gas has no preferred direction of travel?
9701-4.1.1.establish: Gas molecules move continually and collide with the container walls. A molecule that rebounds changes momentum, so it exerts a force on the wall. The combined average force per unit area is the gas pressure. More frequent collisions, or a larger momentum change in each collision, increase the pressure.
9701-4.1.1.connect: This collision picture explains why a gas fills its container and provides the physical meaning of the $p$ used in $pV=nRT$.
9701-4.1.1.note:
- Moving gas molecules collide with container walls.
- A collision changes momentum and exerts force on the wall.
- Pressure is the average wall force per unit area.
9701-4.1.1.self_explain: Explain how a molecular collision with a wall produces pressure, using the words momentum, force and area.

discover.stem: Identify what directly creates pressure on a sealed container wall.

options.A: Collisions of gas molecules with that wall
options.C: The gas molecules having zero mass
options.D: Attraction of the gas to the container centre

discover.explanation: Wall collisions change molecular momentum and exert force on the wall.

9701-4.1.2.motivate: The equation for gases is simple because it starts from an intentionally simplified particle model.
9701-4.1.2.establish: An ideal gas has particles with zero particle volume and no intermolecular forces of attraction. The particles still have mass and move, so they can collide with walls. Real gas particles occupy space and can attract one another. Real gases tend to behave most nearly ideally at high temperature and low pressure: attractions matter less when kinetic energy is high, and particle volume matters less when particles are far apart.
9701-4.1.2.connect: Those assumptions explain when measured real-gas behaviour is closest to the predictions of $pV=nRT$.
9701-4.1.2.note:
- Ideal particles have zero particle volume.
- They have no intermolecular forces of attraction.
- They retain mass and can collide with walls.
- Real gases approximate ideal behaviour best at high temperature and low pressure.
9701-4.1.2.self_explain: State both ideal-gas assumptions and explain why zero particle volume does not mean zero mass.

discover.stem: State which ideal-gas assumption concerns forces between molecules.
discover.explanation: The model neglects intermolecular attraction while retaining moving, massive particles.

9701-4.1.3.motivate: One equation lets you find an unknown gas amount, volume, pressure or even relative molecular mass from measurements.
9701-4.1.3.establish: State the ideal gas equation as $pV=nRT$. Use pressure $p$ in Pa, volume $V$ in m³, amount $n$ in mol, absolute temperature $T$ in K and $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$. Convert cm³ to m³ by multiplying by $10^{-6}$, dm³ to m³ by multiplying by $10^{-3}$, and Celsius temperature to kelvin by adding 273. Rearrange before substituting. For a mass $m$ in grams, $n=m/M_r$, so $M_r=mRT/(pV)$. If gas is produced by a reaction, use the balanced mole ratio after finding the limiting reagent.
9701-4.1.3.connect: The mole concept supplies $n$; the kinetic model explains the pressure and why the equation is approximate for real gases.
9701-4.1.3.note:
- $pV=nRT$ with $R=8.31\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.
- Use Pa, m³, mol and K.
- For gas mass $m$ in grams, $M_r=mRT/(pV)$.
- Apply balanced-equation mole ratios when gas is formed.
9701-4.1.3.self_explain: Derive $M_r=mRT/(pV)$ from $pV=nRT$, then name the SI units needed for $p$, $V$ and $T$.
